claims.claim: Federal policy requires grand and petit juries to be selected at random from a fair cross section of the community, and bars excluding a citizen from federal jury service on account of race, color, religion, sex, national origin, or economic status.

In federal court a challenge for cause requires a stated reason ruled on by the judge, while peremptory challenges are rationed by rule: 20 per side in a capital case, 6 for the government and 10 jointly for the defense in a felony case, and 3 per side in a misdemeanor case.

Batson v. Kentucky (1986) holds that a defendant may make a prima facie case of purposeful discrimination from the facts of his own trial, after which the burden shifts to the State to give a neutral explanation for the strikes, with the trial court deciding whether discrimination has been shown; a prosecutor may not rebut by invoking shared race or his own good faith.

Under Crawford v. Washington (2004), where testimonial statements are at issue the only indicium of reliability sufficient to satisfy the Confrontation Clause is confrontation itself, and police interrogations fall squarely within the testimonial class.
Griffin v. California (1965) holds that a prosecutor may not comment to the jury on a defendant's failure to testify, and a court may not instruct that such silence evidences guilt.

Ramos v. Louisiana, decided April 20, 2020, holds that the Sixth Amendment jury-trial right as incorporated against the states requires a unanimous verdict to convict of a serious offense; before that decision Louisiana and Oregon allowed 10-to-2 verdicts while 48 states and federal court did not.

Federal Rule of Criminal Procedure 31 requires a unanimous verdict returned in open court, permits partial verdicts, allows a mistrial and retrial on counts the jury cannot agree on, and provides for polling the jury.

A federal defendant entitled to a jury trial can be tried without one only if he waives the jury in writing, the government consents, and the court approves; a federal jury is 12 unless the parties stipulate to fewer or the court permits 11 for good cause after deliberations begin.

The jury-trial right does not reach every offense: Duncan v. Louisiana treated a crime punishable by two years as serious without fixing the boundary, Lewis v. United States presumes an offense carrying six months or less to be petty and refuses to aggregate petty charges, and Williams v. Florida holds the Constitution does not fix jury size at 12.

18 U.S.C. 3553(a) tells a federal court to impose a sentence sufficient but not greater than necessary to achieve the purposes in (a)(2): just punishment, deterrence, protection of the public, and needed training, medical care, or other correctional treatment; restitution appears separately at (a)(7), so the fifth purpose usually taught as restoration is not one of the (a)(2) purposes.

States followed an indeterminate model in the early 1970s in which a parole board decided release; pressure for longer and more uniform punishment produced mandatory minimums and sentencing guidelines in the 1980s, and by 1998 truth-in-sentencing incentive grants had gone to 27 states and the District of Columbia. Prisoners released in 1996 served on average 44 percent of their sentences.

United States v. Booker (2005) produced two majorities: one held that the Sixth Amendment as construed in Blakely applies to the Federal Sentencing Guidelines because 18 U.S.C. 3553(b) made them binding, and the other severed and excised 3553(b)(1) and 3742(e), leaving the Guidelines effectively advisory with appellate review for unreasonableness.
In fiscal year 2025, 33,979 of 66,036 federal cases (51.5 percent) were sentenced within the guideline range and 20,577 (31.2 percent) were variances from it.

Apprendi v. New Jersey (2000) requires any fact other than a prior conviction that increases the penalty beyond the prescribed statutory maximum to be found by a jury beyond a reasonable doubt, and Blakely v. Washington (2004) defines that maximum as the most a judge may impose on the facts in the verdict or admitted by the defendant.

18 U.S.C. 924(c) requires a term of at least 5 years, 7 years if a firearm is brandished, and 10 years if it is discharged, in addition to the punishment for the underlying crime of violence or drug trafficking crime; 18 U.S.C. 3553(e) and (f) supply the two routes below a statutory minimum.

Federal Rule 32 requires a probation officer's presentence investigation and report that calculates the offense level, criminal history category and resulting range, disclosed to the parties at least 35 days before sentencing, with objections due within 14 days; before imposing sentence the court must allow the defendant to speak personally and must permit a victim present at sentencing to be reasonably heard.

Under 18 U.S.C. 3584(a) multiple terms of imprisonment imposed at the same time run concurrently unless the court orders, or a statute mandates, that they run consecutively, while terms imposed at different times run consecutively unless the court orders them to run concurrently.

Beyond imprisonment, a federal sentence can include a fine capped by 18 U.S.C. 3571, mandatory restitution under 18 U.S.C. 3663A for the offenses that statute covers, and a term of supervised release under 18 U.S.C. 3583 of up to five, three, or one year depending on offense class.

Furman v. Georgia (1972) invalidated the death sentences before it in a per curiam judgment supported by five separate opinions with four separate dissents, and Gregg v. Georgia (1976) upheld a revised Georgia scheme built on a bifurcated trial, statutory aggravating circumstances found beyond a reasonable doubt, and automatic proportionality review; BJS records that executions resumed in 1977.

Atkins v. Virginia (2002) bars executing offenders with intellectual disability, Roper v. Simmons (2005) bars executing offenders who were under 18 at the time of the crime, and Ring v. Arizona (2002) requires a jury rather than a judge to find the aggravating circumstance that makes a defendant death-eligible.

On December 31, 2022, 30 states and the federal government had death penalty statutes and 21 jurisdictions (20 states and the District of Columbia) did not; 26 states and the Federal Bureau of Prisons held 2,270 prisoners under sentence of death, and six states carried out 18 executions in 2022. In Delaware, New York and Washington the statutes remained on the books after state high courts held portions unconstitutional while capital cases were no longer pursued.

Federal capital sentencing is statutorily bifurcated: after conviction the court holds a separate sentencing hearing, ordinarily before the trial jury, with a 12-member jury when one must be impaneled and with no presentence report prepared.

Of the 2,270 prisoners under sentence of death in the United States at yearend 2022, BJS recorded 1,286 (56.7 percent) as White and 927 (40.8 percent) as Black, counting ethnicity separately with 326 recorded as Hispanic.

conflictingEvidence.issue: How many purposes of punishment there are, and whether federal law recognizes all of them
positions: Criminal justice courses commonly teach five purposes: retribution, deterrence, incapacitation, rehabilitation, and restoration.
18 U.S.C. 3553(a)(2) lists four considerations, and restitution to victims appears separately at 3553(a)(7).
conflictingEvidence.resolution: The lesson teaches the five-purpose vocabulary but states plainly that only four appear in 3553(a)(2) and that restoration enters federal sentencing through restitution provisions rather than through the purposes paragraph. Both statements are sourced to the statute itself.

conflictingEvidence.issue: What Booker actually did to the federal sentencing guidelines
positions: A common shorthand says the Supreme Court struck down the guidelines.
The opinion severed two statutory provisions, 18 U.S.C. 3553(b)(1) and 3742(e), and left the guidelines standing as advisory.
conflictingEvidence.resolution: The bound-volume opinion was read in full. The lesson states the two-majority structure, names the excised provisions, and notes that courts must still calculate and consider the range, which the Sentencing Commission's own materials confirm.

conflictingEvidence.issue: Which bound-volume citation to give for Ramos v. Louisiana
positions: Secondary sources cite Ramos as 590 U.S. 83 (2020).
The govinfo United States Reports package for volume 590 could not be retrieved on 2026-08-19.
conflictingEvidence.resolution: The lesson cites Ramos by docket number (No. 18-5924) and decision date (April 20, 2020) from the Court's own slip opinion, and does not assert a bound-volume page that could not be verified against a primary host.

conflictingEvidence.issue: How to present the demographic composition of the population under sentence of death
positions: The composition is a documented fact that a survey lesson should not omit.
Causal explanations for the composition are contested and are not settled by the counts themselves.
conflictingEvidence.resolution: The lesson reports the BJS counts with their date and states explicitly that they describe what was measured rather than explaining why, and that the causes are contested.

unsupportedExistingClaims: The generated draft contained no substantive assertion about trial or sentencing at all; its body was placeholder text about 'a foundational concept' and a 'toolbox drawer' analogy, none of which was verifiable or usable.
The draft's learning objectives, vocabulary, worked example, mistakes and question bank were all generic templates with no criminal-justice content.
correctionsNeeded: Replaced the entire generated draft with an original lesson built from primary sources.
Stated explicitly that the federal guidelines are advisory after Booker rather than binding, and named the two severed statutory provisions instead of saying the guidelines were 'struck down'.
Distinguished the five purposes taught in the field from the four purposes actually enumerated in 18 U.S.C. 3553(a)(2).
Dated every quantitative figure and attributed it to the issuing agency and publication year.
Cited Ramos v. Louisiana by docket number and decision date rather than an unverified bound-volume page.
Used 'intellectual disability' in the lesson's own voice while noting that the Atkins opinion used the term then current.
rightsIssues: Supreme Court opinions and the United States Code are edicts of government and are treated as public domain; they were read in official bound-volume or Office of the Law Revision Counsel copies.
Bureau of Justice Statistics and U.S. Sentencing Commission publications are treated as REFERENCE_ONLY: facts and figures were extracted, and no agency wording was reproduced.

The Cornell Legal Information Institute copies of 18 U.S.C. 3553 and Lewis v. United States are mirrors registered under ids already in this project's source registry; they are REFERENCE_ONLY for site wording, and the underlying statute and opinion are public domain.
No source's prose was paraphrase-followed; all lesson prose is original.

sourceRecords.license: Judicial opinion; edict of government, not subject to copyright
sourceRecords.notes: Official U.S. Reports bound-volume text downloaded and read in full for the unusual two-majority structure. Of 66,036 fiscal year 2025 federal cases for which the sentence could be compared with the guideline range, 33,979 (51.5 percent) were within the range, 45,459 (68.8 percent) were sentenced under the Guidelines Manual including departures, and 20,577 (31.2 percent) were variances, of which 2,890 (4.4 percent) were upward. Used to show what advisory guidelines look like in practice.

Used for these figures as of December 31, 2022: 30 states and the federal government had death penalty statutes; 21 jurisdictions did not authorize the death penalty (20 states plus the District of Columbia, listed by name); 26 states and the Federal Bureau of Prisons held 2,270 prisoners under sentence of death; and six states executed 18 prisoners during 2022. Also used for the report's notes that Delaware, New York and Washington retained statutes after state high courts held portions unconstitutional while capital cases were no longer pursued, that Oregon's governor commuted 17 death sentences in December 2022, and that Furman effected a moratorium on executions that ended when executions resumed in 1977 after Gregg.

sourceRecords.provider: Bureau of Justice Statistics, U.S. Department of Justice
sourceRecords.notes: Special Report PDF (bjs.ojp.gov/content/pub/pdf/tssp.pdf, reached through this landing page) downloaded and read. Published January 1999 by Paula M. Ditton and Doris James Wilson. Used as a dated historical source for the shift away from indeterminate sentencing: in the early 1970s states followed an indeterminate model in which a parole board decided release, pressure for longer and more uniform punishment produced mandatory minimums and sentencing guidelines in the 1980s, and truth-in-sentencing incentive grants were awarded in 1998 to 27 states and the District of Columbia. Also used for the finding that prisoners released in 1996 served on average 44 percent of their sentence, and that violent offenders released in 1996 had been sentenced to an average of 85 months and served about 45 months.
